rv.q: Jonathan Church’s sleek production goes on to show how incisive the genre can be.
The show is a force field of charm and indelible music.
The sometimes serious mood lifts every time the guys launch into one of the big numbers in Jonathan Church’s slick and snazzy production.

…Jukebox musicals have not been underdone on the West End, and The Drifters Girl adds to the canon. I rather enjoyed it. Beverley Knight plays Faye Treadwell, the teacher who in 1957 married a music impresario and later became manager of his biggest group, the Drifters.
The music is glorious, the performances terrific
Yet the dramatic balance doesn’t feel quite right yet.
It’s the script that doesn’t quite work at the moment.
As a musical it flails, but every time the quartet layers up those coil-tight harmonies, or Knight lets rip, it’s heaven.

From the group’s earliest incarnation in the mid-1950s as Clyde McPhatter and the Drifters, that beguiling blend of soul and doo-wop produced hits, although arguably not quite enough of the instantly recognisable headline hits that are required to sustain a West End jukebox musical.
Ultimately, however, the musical numbers feel tacked on and unrelated to the action that’s just played out before us.
But oh dear, Ed Curtis’s script is awful, full of clunking exposition and bathos.
But this show, directed by Jonathan Church, relies on that catalogue of songs too heavily, which compromises the narrative journey and emotional force.
But I couldn’t help but find ‘The Drifters Girl’ a bit tawdry.
The sheer exuberance of the production turns it into an extraordinarily enjoyable night out in the theatre.
Luckily, musically The Drifters Girl is worth the price of admission alone.
The Drifters Girl isn't going to change anybody's life, and to be honest it's unlikely to become anyone's favourite musical.
The Drifters Girl, ultimately, is a mixed bag.
However, Ed Curtis’s book is rather less pioneering; in fact, it falls into all the worst traps of jukebox bio-musicals.
Beverley Knight and her hugely talented co-stars deliver sensational pop perfection in this jukebox musical based on the 1960s band and their indomitable manager.

cn.t: A crowd-pleasing jukebox musical elevated by powerhouse vocals from Beverley Knight and co-stars delivering classic Drifters hits, though critics find the script and biographical focus on manager Faye Treadwell uneven.
